newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Controversial Kazakh airline in Delhi crash.
newsitem.headline: Controversial Kazakh airline in Delhi crash.

text.p: The Kazakh cargo plane which collided in mid-air on Tuesday with a Saudi jumbo jet near Delhi belonged to an airline with huge debts and a controversial safety record.
There was no clue by early Wednesday of what caused the world's worst mid-air catastrophe, feared to have claimed some 350 lives. Any number of factors may have contributed.
Flight 1907 was the latest of many from the economically depressed former Soviet Union to meet disaster in recent years.

The state airline which Kazakh and Indian officials said owned the doomed Ilyushin Il-76TD freighter has been dogged by financial problems. It was formally closed down in August after being criticised by the government for falling safety standards.
The crashed plane, registered number 76435, was chartered from Kazakhstan National Airways, known as KazAir, by a firm in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, a Kazakh transport official said.
It took off from Chimkent in southern Kazakhstan for Delhi with 10 crew and 28 passengers, many of them Kyrgyz nationals.

In August, Kazakhstan National Airways, one of hundreds of "babyflots" spawned by the break-up of Aeroflot as the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, had been formally closed down after running up $149 million in debts.

The Almaty government announced a new national airline, Air Kazakhstan, would take over KazAir's operations. An official inquiry had criticised its management and found its planes badly serviced and close to failing international safety norms.
An international aviation insurance expert told Reuters recently that some airlines from Kazakhstan had difficulty obtaining international insurance cover because of safety fears.
One of KazAir's Tupolev Tu-154 passenger jets caught fire on take-off at Kiev in July. No one was hurt.
Cash shortages and cut-throat competition have been blamed for falling airline safety standards across Moscow's old empire.
Aircraft manufacturers defend their products and blame poor maintenance and overstretched crews for problems.
Ilyushin 76s, four-engined loadbearers common in the former Soviet fleet and now chartered extensively by cost-conscious foreign operators, have suffered a number of recent accidents.
One owned by a private Russian firm crashed at Belgrade in August as the pilot attempted an emergency landing. All 10 crew aboard were killed.
In June, a Ukrainian Il-76 crashed on take-off at Kinshasa in Zaire, again killing the 10-man crew. In April, 12 died when an Il-76 came down on the far eastern Kamchatka peninsula.

Kinshasa was the site of one of the world's worst air crashes when, in January this year, a Russian Antonov An-32 ploughed into a crowded marketplace shortly after take-off. Some 350 were killed. Two Russian pilots are in a Zairean jail.
A Russian An-124 freighter came down on houses near Turin last month, killing two of the crew and two Italian villagers.
In general, there has been much greater loss of life involving passenger aircraft.
More than 140 people, mostly Ukrainian coalminers and their families, died when a Russian Tupolev Tu-154 slammed into a mountain on Norway's Arctic island of Spitsbergen in August.
The U.S. Federal Aviation Authority said last December after the crash of a Tu-154 in the Far East that Russian airlines were "minimally meeting requirements" for international air safety.
The most notorious crash of recent years was in March 1994, when 70 people died after an Aeroflot pilot allowed his teenage son to send an Airbus A310 crashing into the Siberian taiga.
